claims.text: Heating sub-10 nm Au-Co-Cu-Ni-Pt nanoparticles from 300 K to 1000 K causes structural evolution driven by surface-energy minimization and thermodynamic phase separation rather than sluggish diffusion.
The sluggish-diffusion assumption breaks down below 10 nm because of the high surface-to-volume ratio.
Surface diffusion is orders of magnitude faster than bulk diffusion in this nanoparticle system and therefore dominates its kinetics.
Positive mixing enthalpies for pairs such as Au-Cu or Pt-Cu provide a thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
The high surface energy of the smallest particles amplifies the driving force for phase separation.
The loss of the smallest particles occurs through Ostwald ripening.
During Ostwald ripening, smaller particles dissolve to feed larger particles, reducing total surface energy.
Particle faceting or irregularity results from anisotropic surface diffusion rates.
Au or Pt preferentially segregates to nanoparticle surfaces, while Co and Cu segregate to the core or form precipitates.
For sub-10 nm particles, the surface-energy term dominates the Gibbs free energy.
Surface-diffusion activation energies are sufficiently lower than bulk-diffusion activation energies to permit rapid atomic rearrangement in this alloy.
Particles smaller than 5 nm will be rapidly lost within the first 100-200 K of heating.
Heating will produce core-shell structures with Au/Pt-enriched surfaces and Co/Cu/Ni-enriched cores.
Heating will produce significant particle faceting.
At 1000 K, the nanoparticles will not remain a stable single-phase solid solution and will instead contain phase-separated domains or precipitates.
The average particle size will increase by a factor of two to three relative to the initial size.
The high-entropy-alloy baseline predicts a single-phase solid solution with little grain growth or phase separation because of configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion.
For particles larger than 50 nm, bulk diffusion may become rate-limiting and sluggish diffusion may delay phase separation.
Oxygen exposure would introduce oxidation mechanisms that could alter the vacuum-heating outcome.
The initial equiatomic nanoparticles are likely a disordered solid solution or another metastable state.
